```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_scip <- requireNamespace("scip", quietly = TRUE)
has_osqp <- requireNamespace("osqp", quietly = TRUE)
has_nloptr <- requireNamespace("nloptr", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(optcompR)
```

optcompR describes an optimization problem once, as variables, expressions,
constraints and an objective, and then classifies it, chooses a capable solver
This tutorial explains the distinctions that decide which solver applies and
how to read its result, with a small model for each.

## Convex and nonconvex

A problem is convex when it minimizes a convex function (or maximizes a
concave one) over a convex set. Every local minimum of a convex problem is
global. `opt_classify()` decides convexity for polynomial models of degree two
and records how:

```{r}
m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2)
opt_objective(m, x[1]^2 + x[1] * x[2] + x[2]^2)
cl <- opt_classify(m)
cl$convexity
cl$evidence
opt_objective(m, x[1]^2 + 3 * x[1] * x[2] + x[2]^2)
opt_classify(m)$convexity
```

For general nonlinear expressions convexity is reported as `unknown`; it is
not guessed.

## Continuous and mixed-integer

Integer variables make the feasible set a union of points or slices. The LP
relaxation gives a bound, and branch and bound closes the gap:

```{r}
m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, type = "integer", lower = 0)
opt_constraint(m, 2 * x[1] + 2 * x[2] <= 7)
opt_objective(m, x[1] + x[2])
r_int <- opt_solve(m)
opt_set_type(m, x, "continuous")
r_lp <- opt_solve(m)
c(integer = opt_objective_value(r_int), relaxation = opt_objective_value(r_lp))
```

## Local and global optima

```{r, eval = has_nloptr}
m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", lower = -3, upper = 3, start = 2)
opt_objective(m, x^4 - 4 * x^2 + x)
r <- opt_solve(m, solver = "nloptr")
c(x = opt_value(r, x), f = opt_objective_value(r))
opt_status(r)
opt_set_start(m, x, -2)
r2 <- opt_solve(m, solver = "nloptr")
c(x = opt_value(r2, x), f = opt_objective_value(r2))
```

Different starts end in different local minima, and the status says
`locally_optimal`, never `optimal`.

## Feasible and optimal

A feasible point satisfies every constraint; an optimal point is feasible and
has the best objective. Solvers stopped by limits may return a feasible point
that is not proven optimal; `opt_has_solution()`, `opt_status()` and
`opt_gap()` together tell which case applies.

## Primal and dual

The primal variables are the decisions $x$. The dual variables $y$ price the
constraints: $y_i = \partial f^* / \partial b_i$. In optcompR this sign
convention holds for both minimization and maximization, and
`opt_check()` verifies the KKT stationarity condition
$\nabla f(x) - J(x)^\top y - z = 0$.

## Termination and solution status

`opt_status()` reports why the solver stopped (`optimal`, `infeasible`,
`time_limit`, ...). `opt_primal_status()` and `opt_dual_status()` report
whether the returned vectors are feasible. A `time_limit` termination with a
`feasible_point` primal status is a usable incumbent.

## Derivatives and sensitivity of optima

The gradient of the objective, $\nabla f(x)$, describes the model function.
The sensitivity of the optimum, $\partial f^* / \partial b$, describes the
optimization problem as a whole; by the envelope theorem it equals the dual.
See `vignette("sensitivity")`.
